---
title: "Mathematical detail"
---

`PowerUtilityModel` uses the formulas below, and the notation follows
Mehra and Prescott (1985).

## Endowment

Annual consumption growth is a two-state Markov chain. Gross growth in
the two states is

$$
\lambda_1 = 1+\mu+\sigma, \qquad \lambda_2 = 1+\mu-\sigma,
$$

The chain has symmetric transitions $\Pr(\lambda_i\to\lambda_i)=\varphi=(1+\rho)/2$
and $\Pr(\lambda_i\to\lambda_j)=1-\varphi$, so the stationary weights are
$(1/2, 1/2)$. The default values $\mu=0.018$, $\sigma=0.036$, and
$\rho=-0.14$ match US per-capita consumption from 1889 to 1978.

## Kernel

Power utility $u(C)=C^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$ gives the kernel

$$
M_j = \delta\,\lambda_j^{-\gamma}.
$$

The kernel in state $j$ depends only on consumption growth in state $j$.

## Equity

The Lucas tree pays the endowment, and the price-dividend ratio $q$
solves

$$
q_i = \sum_j \pi_{ij}\, \delta\,\lambda_j^{-\gamma}\, \lambda_j\, (q_j+1).
$$

Gross return from $i$ to $j$ is $\lambda_j(q_j+1)/q_i$, and the bill in
state $i$ is $1/\sum_j \pi_{ij} M_j$. Unconditional means of both
returns are averages under the stationary distribution.

For a levered claim, $\lambda_j$ in the payoff is replaced with
$\lambda_j^{\phi}$, and the claim is equity when $\phi=1$.

## The puzzle

Mehra and Prescott search $\gamma\in(0,10]$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, and
the pairs they obtain never match the sample pair $(E[R_f], E[R_e]-E[R_f]) \approx
(0.80\%, 6.18\%)$. A high value of $\gamma$ raises the premium only by
raising the bill.

The sources are Mehra and Prescott (1985) and Cochrane, *Asset Pricing*,
chapter 1.
